utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technicians, interpreters; good morning, legal assistant, registry; good morning, counsel for the Prosecution, counsel for the Defence. Good morning to you, General Krstic. We will be continuing with your testimony. Let me remind you that you are still testifying under oath. And without much further ado, I will give the floor to Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel, and General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, we left off yesterday discussing the convoys that were to come in to the Srebrenica enclave, and I believe you had explained that the Main Staff was the one that determined whether or not the convoys were allowed to go into the Srebrenica enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it was the job of the Drina Corps to implement the orders of the Main Staff in that regard, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the liaison officer of the Main Staff, the liaison officer with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You received the communication from the Main Staff regarding which convoy could or could not go into the enclave; is that right? The Drina Corps received that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally never received any such messages or orders to that effect. I mean while I was the Chief of Staff. I don't think that there was any single case involving a convoy entry to the protected area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was the liaison officer for the Drina Corps for the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only during these proceedings that I realised that it was actually Major Nikolic who was an assistant commander to the Bratunac Brigade commander. He was an assistant for intelligence and security affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What position did -- I believe it's Lieutenant Colonel Vukovic -- have from the Skelani Separate Battalion, if I'm not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic was the commander of the Pribicevac Technical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: According to Colonel Karremans, Colonel Vukovic was one of the principal liaison officers along with Major Nikolic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that piece of information. I remember when he was testifying, I remember that Colonel Karremans was talking about a meeting that they attended -- whether it was in February or April, I don't remember -- that they were together at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge of Colonel Vukovic being the liaison officer for that battalion?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were convoys allowed into the Srebrenica enclave after the end of April 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the situation regarding the Muslim population and their conditions regarding food in the enclave after April 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to Exhibit 122A, and I believe 122B should be the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you could, General, go to the little green tab, the first one in the group, and there should be an area that is highlighted on the first green tab, and I will briefly try to read this and ask you whether or not you believe it's credible. It starts out --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we put the English on the ELMO? It's page number 63 in the English. For the record, this is the testimony of Colonel Thomas Karremans at the Rule 61 hearing that was played as part of this trial. All right. I first want to start with that paragraph at -- is that page 63? If you can hand that to me, I can straighten that out. 122A, the English version, page 63. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I will start to quote: "At the end of April the real convey terror, as we called it in those days, started because as of 26th of April no convoy came in at all." And then going down the page, I believe Mr. Harmon asked the question: 4 "Q. What effect did this have on the civilian -- did the Bosnian Serb blockade have on the civilian population within the enclave? "A. Yes, sir, it did, because almost, let us say, 25.000 persons living in the enclave were refugees, as there used to live about 8.000 in the village of Srebrenica. So you can imagine that the civil authorities had a mighty challenge to bring under all those refugees in a city with infrastructure for only 8.000 persons. But also the food for all the people living in the enclave was a problem, because the UNHCR was responsible, or at least they were responsible, for bringing in the food. Also the UNHCR had the same problems with getting in their food for the inhabitants of the enclave." Now, if we could turn to what has been marked as page 2. Do you see that? Or 1870. Mr. Harmon goes on to say: "MR. HARMON: Thank you, Your Honour. Colonel Karremans, yesterday you described the Bosnian Serb Army blockade that slowly strangled the enclave as a convoy of terror. What effect did this have on the occupants in the enclave? "A. I would like to stipulate some things which I have said yesterday concerning the circumstances, I must say the miserable circumstances, for the inhabitants of the enclave, but also for my own Battalion. That could explain something on the circumstances up to 6th July. Those, let us say, miserable circumstances in April, May and June were caused, what I said yesterday, by refusing the incoming convoys, either for the battalion or by UNHCR for the refugees. Thus, we had to do with a strangulation of the enclave or, so to call, an isolation, a total blockade. "That meant for the population, for instance, that their situation was poorer than poor. There was starvation for the refugees. Some died by the starvation. There was no medical treatment at all for the population, no doctors, no dentists, no medicines. MSF was not able to fulfil its job in the local hospital. We could not do anything about infrastructure to support the local authorities like housing, like generators, power and electricity and water supply for the population. "It ended up, for instance, that hundreds of inhabitants of the enclave lived literally on the garbage collection point. There was no travel allowed both for the population and for the Battalion. What was agreed in the beginning in 1993, so-called freedom of movement, there was no freedom of movement at all. "Our conclusion for the inhabitants, the population of enclave, was that the situation was hopeless, inhuman and a lot of suffering for the people." General Krstic, do you have any reason to believe this is not a credible statement by Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. McCloskey. The second part that you have just read out, I cannot find it in B/C/S. I don't even know what page it is on. As to the portion that was marked with this green tab, I believe that that indeed refers to the issue you've brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, if you could take a moment. The second green tab is the second piece that I read. So if you start with the second green tab, and it should also be highlighted for you.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware that people in the enclave were starving to death at this time in May and June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't know that. I wasn't familiar with the situation. As to the description given here by Colonel Karremans, I can, therefore, offer no comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go back to Krivaja 95, if we could. Exhibit 428A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General Krstic, just concerning your no comment on it, what does that mean? You don't know about it?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply wasn't familiar with that. I have already said that, as regards convoys and other similar matters related to the protected area, that that was under the jurisdiction of the Main Staff. At that time, at the beginning those events, I was still undergoing treatment. Later on, I was busy with the issues concerning the front line. So I don't have any knowledge as regards the situation in Srebrenica involving the civilian population and the supply of food and other aid to the civilian population within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So the answer is that you have no knowledge? Is that the answer?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, did you have to consider in planning for Krivaja 95 the possible military activities of NATO and NATO forces and their possible intervention?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time we were planning the operation, and at the beginning of the operation, whose purpose was to separate the two enclaves, we did not take into account the possibility of military activities of NATO and NATO forces from air. Our starting point was that the act of separating the two enclaves was a legitimate one and that we were not doing anything that would possibly endanger the civilian population and the protected area itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever make a plan or incorporate in this plan, Krivaja 95 -- well, I'm sorry. Let me start over with that question. Did you ever incorporate into this plan the possibility of intervention by NATO forces?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In each order, so as in this one as well, it is envisaged that a battle may occur involving targets in the air. The order makes mention of measures that need to be undertaken in case of NATO airstrikes, but we had completely ruled out the possibility of the NATO airstrike during the operation of separating the two enclaves, Zepa and Srebrenica. This is simply one item of the order which concerns anti-aircraft defence. Like I said, each order, not only this one concerning the Krivaja 95 operation, so each order has to make mention in this way the possibility of airstrikes, and this is the way that it is always written.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this order does anticipate what you should do, what the VRS forces should do in the event of intervention by NATO forces?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it is only envisaging the possibility of airstrikes. It was actually not a real possibility for us, because we thought that our aim was a legitimate one, and we didn't even count with the airstrikes. And at the time the operation to separate the two enclaves was launched until the final aim was realised, there were no airstrikes by NATO forces. The attack came later on, after the order was issued to continue with the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that this was a very serious document. Is there paragraphs or material in this document, Krivaja 95, that are completely unimportant and not applicable, and are just, as you've suggested, a matter of something you always have to fill out when writing one of these orders?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything is important in this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the event of an airborne assault by NATO, whose job was it to take on the airborne NATO troops under this order?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every unit had certain devices for combat with targets that were airborne, starting from 20- and 30-millimetre guns and Strela 2-M. However, those resources are not effective when it comes to medium- and long-range targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What I meant to ask was: How does this plan anticipate NATO troops landing on the ground, either from the air, from either helicopters or parachutes? Who is supposed to deal with NATO troops under this plan?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you been able to find that section in the report? I can refer you to paragraph 9 in the -- excuse me -- in the order.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I've found the paragraph. It is paragraph 9 of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it basically says that if NATO forces make an airborne landing in support of UNPROFOR, the units closest to the landing place and reserve forces will engage in combat with them. So this plan anticipates the reserve forces taking on any NATO forces that land in this manner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't apply only to reserve forces, but all the units engaged on the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But it certainly anticipates the reserve forces as well as, like it says, the people that they happen to land on top of?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if there are any reserves, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You listened to General Dannatt's testimony about reserves and the importance of reserves, and I know you've received training and experience. It's important to have reserve forces in any military operation, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did envisage them, but this order was not handed to forces that we had in reserve because we thought we wouldn't need them. But they were anticipated, and not one of the officers whose forces were to be in the reserve received this order, nor did they know that the operation was being prepared, planned, and that it would be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we go to page 5 of Krivaja 95, we can see those reserve forces are noted in their own paragraph. "Reserve forces ..." and I'm reading now, and it's under paragraph 5 also, General: "Reserve forces of a size of two or three companies of the MUP, and one company from the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade." Those MUP forces in Vlasenica and one company from the Vlasenica Brigade were the reserve forces as set out in this plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were envisaged, but this order was never handed to them, as can be seen at the end of this order, when the units to whom this order was handed are listed on page 6. And it says: Forward command post of the Drina Corps, the 1st Zvornik Brigade, the 1st Birac Brigade, the 2nd Romanija Brigade, the 1st Bratunac Brigade, the 1st Milici Brigade, and the 5th Platoon. So not a single of the units which were envisaged to be the reserve force received this order, nor did we, while carrying out the task assigned to us by the commander of the Drina Corps, have such reserves, nor did we think that we would need to deploy them and engage them in battle. It was only in the 11th, in the afternoon, upon orders by General Mladic, that the order was given to strengthen the attack from the direction that the Bratunac Brigade should have attacked on -- and I spoke about this earlier on in my testimony -- because we had a lot of problems with a part of that brigade which was engaged in the attack. In the afternoon of the 11th, the order was given that some units, about 50 or 60 men, should be brought from the Vlasenica Brigade, and they were brought there, and they were deployed along the route Kak-Guber Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know a MUP officer named Dusko Jevdic, nickname or code name Stalin, who was a man identified as being in Potocari on July 12th near Mladic's entourage?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard of that man, and, particularly, I never heard of such a nickname either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this section of the report makes a reference to two or three companies. How many soldiers would be envisioned in a company of this kind?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the numerical strength of those units of the MUP. I am not familiar with their organisational structure. An Infantry Company in a Light Brigade in the army numbered between 80 and 100 men. As for MUP unit strength and their organisational structure in terms of numbers, it's something I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would the commanders that received this report be able to tell how many men there were in reserve for them or would they be like you, they wouldn't know?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In receipt of this report, a commander would naturally look to see how many reserves he had, and would a commander, when they read the size of two or three companies, get at least some sort of an estimate of how many men would be backing him up in reserve?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the commanders to whom this order was forwarded, they don't care which units are in reserve. What is important for them are their forces because here, in the order, it is not stated from which axis the reserve forces would be brought, what their tasks will be, which unit which was attacking up to a certain line would be replaced by those reserves. So this is not stated anywhere in this order to unit commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let me call your attention to the reserve section. In the next paragraph right under the reserve section, it says "Task," and there is a listing of tasks, and one of them says, "To prevent an enemy withdrawal."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Usher, it's page 5, sorry, in the English translation, of the exhibit Krivaja 95, 428A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, do you consider the exodus of the 28th Division from the Srebrenica enclave on July 11th and 12th an enemy withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not give the matter any thought except in regard to the order of the commander, the Corps Commander for active combat, the order for active combat. It was our assessment that the forces of the 28th Division would only withdraw from the area in between the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa to behind the lines Guber Banja, Zivkovo Brdo, Alibegovac, Kak. We did not even take into consideration the possibility of the forces of the 28th Division as a whole because of our efforts to achieve this aim given in this order that they would withdraw from the same area, because there was no reason for them to do so in terms of the order of the Drina Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, it's the submission of the Prosecution that the MUP forces were designated as the reserves for their Krivaja 95 operation and that upon the withdrawal of the 28th Division from the enclave, those MUP forces were incorporated into the operation and placed along the Bratunac-Milici road, as we have seen in the video. Do you contest that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not know who ordered first the bringing in of MUP forces and especially the special detachment from the MUP Brigade to the area of Bratunac on the 11th. I never addressed any such request to anyone nor did I make such proposal. And I think that the Commander of the Drina Corps didn't do that either, because those forces arrived on the 11th. I and the command of the Drina Corps never addressed such a request to the Main Staff, but it is a fact, as we have seen on videotape, that those forces did appear blockading the road between Konjevic Polje and Kravica in the early morning hours of the 12th and later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did those MUP forces that arrived on the 11th in Bratunac, where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they came from. I don't know where that unit was located. But they appeared there on the 11th. And General Mladic spoke about this at a meeting with the Command of the Bratunac Brigade when he said, among other things, that a detachment of the special MUP forces had come to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In planning this operation, are you aware of anyone speaking to the MUP and letting them know that they were going to be put in this plan as reserves? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who put in this section about the MUP being reserves?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Corps Commander envisaged a reserve force, and he counted on some MUP forces, should they be necessary. But I would like to repeat, until his idea was put into effect, and that was in the morning of the 10th, there was absolutely no need to engage any unit from the reserve force, not just MUP units but the company from the Vlasenica Brigade was not needed either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned that Obrad Vicic, the operations officer, played a major role in drafting this document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, there is, I believe, a Colonel Slavko Ognjenovic who was also in operations at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any officer with a surname Redjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. That was my pronunciation. I'll try it again. Slavko Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Slavko Ognjenovic. He was an officer in the section for morale, legal, and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he assist in the drafting of this plan in any way?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why would he? Only when it comes to moral support, together with his superior officer Colonel Cerovic, that is possible that he may have participated with respect to that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was Colonel Ognjenovic present in the Vlasenica area during the assault on Srebrenica from July 5th through the 13th?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His superior officer, Colonel Cerovic, must know about that. He was probably at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One other question about Krivaja 95 and we'll move on. Is there anything in this plan that envisaged the continuing of the assault, if advantageous circumstances allow it?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that yesterday in response to your question, to explain the term "the elimination of the enclave," "to create conditions for the elimination of the enclave." To that end, there may be a task specified. And then it says: In the next assignment, attack along such an axis and reach such-and-such a line, in the event that the 28th Division continues to carry out combat operations to engage in sabotage activities, as it had done previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does that envision a whole new attack plan and a whole separate assault, or could this plan have the same forces that are involved in the initial assault just continue on through?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to a later time period and to some other forces, probably stronger forces than those that were engaged to carry out the order of the commander for combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will refer you again to the section of the reserve forces, but this time just above the section of the reserve forces. It's the page 5 of Krivaja, and it states: "In case of advantageous development of the situation, be in readiness for an attack on and in pursuit of the enemy along the aforementioned axis." Is that the separate attack that you've just testified about or something else?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a separate attack envisaged for some later time, for some future time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: General Krstic, I have one question on Krivaja 95 before we leave it. What do you think Krivaja 95 would have anticipated if the Muslim 28th Division simply retreated? Just once the -- once your forces had begun, if they simply retreated toward Muslim-held territory, just fled, did Krivaja 95 anticipate that you would follow, pursue in attack mode, or just let them go? If they just turn on their heels and fled towards Muslim-held territory, what do you think Krivaja 95 anticipated should be the reaction of your forces?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to Krivaja 95 and the 28th Division, we envisaged that the forces of the 28th Division would simply take up positions in front of the line designated in the Drina Corps Commander's order, and that is Guber Banja, Zivkovo Brdo, Alibegovac, and the feature Kak. We never even thought about the possibility that the forces of the 28th Division would pull out, would withdraw from the Srebrenica enclave and make breakthroughs along different directions, because they simply had no need to do that, because our task was simply to separate the two enclaves and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So any reaction you would have to their withdrawing and moving toward Muslim-held territory would have to be the result of another set of orders? There would have to be new orders given as to what to do, apart from Krivaja 95, is that what you're saying, should the Muslim forces start withdrawing and moving out of Srebrenica toward Muslim-held territory? Is that right? Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A new operation would have to be planned. A number of other documents would have to be drafted which would accompany the implementation of that new order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Krstic, I too have a question. I should like to go back to the question of reserve forces. If I understood correctly, you participated in the planning of this operation; is that true?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in the plan, you defined tasks for the reserve forces, involving two or three companies. There is something I don't understand. How can you assign tasks to a force whose size you are not aware of?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not clearly specify the tasks of the reserve forces. We didn't deliver the order to them precisely because their tasks were not specified. It is only in general terms that the potential task of the reserve forces was defined, but it is not stated here which units they are, nor where they should come, nor the axes along which they should act. So no details are given which would have been required had this order been delivered to them. Then you would have to tell them, "You will be deployed in such-and-such a place," or "Go from this region to another region and carry out such-and-such a task."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General Krstic, just -- you were referring more than once to the fact that your task and your plan was to separate the two enclaves. You mentioned before that -- you said, "Our starting point was to separate the two enclaves," and you repeated it right now. And then you mentioned before, "We were not doing anything that would endanger the civilian population." So you are speaking -- you were not a General at that time, were you?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you were participating in the planning?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You were part of the process?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. McCloskey, it is time for a break, so we're going to have a 15-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us resume. Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, I would now like to get into an area we touched upon briefly yesterday, and that is your leadership role in the attack on Srebrenica and its aftermath. You told us that you were at some point surprised to find out that you would be at the forward command post and that General Zivanovic was going to be back at the headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards this particular operation, the implementation of the Corps Commander's decision, I was indeed designated by him to monitor and control the activities until the final completion of the task, but that was not the first time. Earlier on, when I was at Treskavica, I was at the Osmaci post in the area of responsibility of the Birac Brigade. The objective was to crash the offensive of the BH army, in particular, its 2nd Corps. So this was not the first time for me to remain at the command post and General Zivanovic to go in the field, regardless of the task that was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it was your job to be in the front command post and monitor and control the activities of the battle?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task at the Pribicevac forward command post was to monitor the bringing in of the Drina Corps units that were deployed for the purposes of that operation to specific areas, to monitor the beginning of the attack, the course of the attack until the final completion of the decision of the Drina Corps Commander, that is, until the indicated line, Guber Banja, Zivkovo Brdo, Alibegovac, Kak feature was taken up. I reported there on the commander of the Drina Corps all the time, and I kept receiving orders from him as to what to do in the situation when the attack is not going according to the plan's dynamics for the reasons that I mentioned during my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what date did you actually begin your function at the Pribicevac command post?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Pribicevac command post, I began my function upon my arrival there, that is, on the 5th of July in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you continue that function in the days following?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On July 9th, the plan changed, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were not any particular changes in the plan on the 9th of July, the simple reason that the Drina Corps units that were deployed in that operation were still far from the completion of the assignment which was given to them by the Corps Commander in his decision, that is, none of the features designated by the Drina Corps Commander in his decision had not been reached yet [as interpreted]. The feature Kak -- the Kak feature, the Alibegovac feature, except that in the evening hours on that day, the Zivkovo Brdo feature was indeed reached. However, due to an attack that was launched by the forces of the 28th Division, the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade was pushed back from Zivkovo Brdo during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you stay during the night while you were at the Pribicevac command post between the 6th and the 9th?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I slept at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you sure you didn't go back to Bratunac because of your leg or for any other reason?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure about that, but most of the nights I stayed at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When was the decision made, as far as you're aware, to change the plan and actually continue the attack on to the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of July, in the morning or sometime around noon, the commanders of all the units that were engaged in the operation reported that they had completed the assigned task. The 1st Battalion, which was under the command of Lieutenant Vinko Pandurevic, reported that it had regained control of Zivkovo Brdo, whereas the 2nd Battalion, commanded by Colonel Andric, reported that they had also completed their task, and then together with the unit of Colonel Trivic, they had managed to take possession of the Kak and Alibegovac features. At the time of their reports of the completion of their tasks, both General Mladic and General Zivanovic were at the forward command post. General Mladic called all of the commanders, and he told them that they had not completed their assignment. He said, "Panorama 1 here," and he said that the attack towards Srebrenica should be continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you received a document from General Tolimir prior to that on the same subject, on July 9th?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that a document did arrive late in the evening of the 9th of July, and on that day, in the afternoon of that day, General Mladic and General Zivanovic, in addition to General Gvero, had arrived to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit 432A and B provided to the General. This is a July 9 communication to the Drina Corps, to Generals Gvero and Krstic personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, I should like to draw your attention to the need to indicate precisely for the usher the page and the paragraph of the document so that the technical booth can broadcast the document for the public, including, of course, the relevant portion of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Hopefully these will be easier, as opposed to being in the middle of the documents. This is a one-page document. And if we could just -- yes, thank you. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And General Krstic, do you have the B/C/S version of that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could take a moment to read it to perhaps help refresh your recollection. Just let me know, if you can, when you're finished so I can ask you some questions, but take your time if you need it. I think, like you said, this was, according to the stamp, was received at 2350 hours on the 9th. But as you can tell from the second paragraph, this paragraph indicates that, and I'll quote, "That the Drina Corps ..." Excuse me. I had better start from the beginning. "The president of Republika Srpska has been informed of successful combat operations around Srebrenica by units of the Drina Corps and that they have achieved results which enable them to occupy the very town of Srebrenica." Now, you've just testified that by the 9th that hadn't been done yet. Do you think this is correct or was your recollection correct about this -- when the objectives were achieved that allowed this change of direction?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By this time, as regards the receipt of this document from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska -- and the time indicated was 2350 -- nothing was happening to enable us to conclude that the attack can be continued towards Srebrenica. As I have already said, none of the features that were designated in the commander's order were not yet taken up [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you explain the conclusions based that General Tolimir is making in this letter in the first two paragraphs, on the evening of the 9th?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably the reports coming from the Main Staff during the combat operations were also forwarded to the Supreme Command for the attention of the president, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who would have been sending those reports?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From the zone of operation where the battle is going on.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the zone of operation, the reports were going to the Drina Corps command, to the attention of the commander, and the Main Staff. That was customary. That is how we reported during the crushing of the offensive of the BH army, which was conducted from the directions of Tuzla and Kladanj. So this was not the first time that the reports were going from a particular zone of operation, both to the Drina Corps command and the Main Staff. There was an established line of reporting from the forward command post to the command post of the Drina Corps and the Main Staff, and further on from the Main Staff to the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe you've testified that General Mladic is the one on July 10th that made the decision to continue the attack on Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic and General Zivanovic arrived at the Pribicevac forward command post in the afternoon of the 9th of July. They were there on the 10th as well, and he ordered that the operation towards Srebrenica be continued. He also ordered that the troops enter the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that order by General Mladic to continue the operation on to Srebrenica pursuant to this communication from General Tolimir or separate and apart?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladic did not order the operation to continue. He took over command over all commanders and gave them individual commands for the continuation after he introduced himself and issued the order. But it is true that this order of his is linked to this document which General Tolimir sent to the Drina Corps forward command, to General Gvero and me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it is this order, Exhibit 432, reflecting the wishes of President Karadzic that initiated General Mladic's actions to move this operation on to the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether this was prompted by the order or the wish of President Karadzic to continue the attack into the town of Srebrenica is something that one could discuss, but it is quite clear that when General Mladic appeared on the 9th on Pribicevac and later on, his intentions were quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: If I may, let me just ask one question. General, in the second paragraph, it says the President is satisfied with the results and has agreed with the continuation of operations, which certainly suggests that somebody has recommended to him, if he's agreed with the continuation of operations. Do you have any knowledge as to who would have made the specific recommendation to the President that he agreed with?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably that such a recommendation was given to him by General Mladic, but I am truly surprised, because the units, at this point in time, the units of the Drina Corps, had not accomplished the task assigned to them by the Drina Corps Commander in his order. I said that they had still not captured the designated features with the exception of Zivkovo Brdo on the 9th, and the forces of the 28th Division, during the night, launched a counter-attack and pushed back that unit from that feature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just a follow-up question. Do I understand from your testimony that prior to the time that General Mladic, in your words, took over and gave individual commands to the units to go on through and enter Srebrenica, that you were not personally consulted for your advice as to whether that was a wise course of action militarily to take? In other words, did General Mladic go ahead and make that order to the individual unit commands without ever asking you your opinion or advice?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me for my opinion nor did they consult me. Whether General Mladic, on the road from Jezernica to Pribicevac, did discuss this with General Zivanovic, I really don't know, but the early arrival of General Gvero at the forward command post, and later the arrival of General Mladic and General Zivanovic, spoke for such intentions, because after receiving this document from the Main Staff and also the next day, on the 10th, the order was given to continue the attack, so General Mladic's intentions were quite clear as regards the continuation of the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, I note that this letter from General Tolimir is addressed to the forward command post, to you and General Gvero personally. Now, if General Mladic and General Zivanovic were at the forward command post on July 9th, why is it that you are getting this personally as opposed to them?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether General Tolimir knew that General Zivanovic and General Mladic would come to the forward command post in the afternoon of the 9th, but he certainly did know that we were there, that is, General Gvero and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So prior to General Mladic's arrival at the forward command post, you had been the person in control of the battle plan and the operation at the forward command post; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Until the afternoon of the 9th when General Mladic and General Zivanovic arrived, I reported regularly about all problems encountered in the course of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Brigade Commanders who had been leading the assault reported to you at least daily, if not more, during that assault; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until that date, the afternoon of the 9th. They reported to me not through written reports but using radio communications, RUP 12, which was fully encrypted, so that I knew at every point in time where the units were, what line they had reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So by the afternoon of July 9th, you, as the Chief of Staff in control of this battle, had more knowledge than anyone else of how it was going.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite so. I said that I sent reports about this. We had very great problems. The assault was not progressing as we had expected because of the configuration of the land, because of the very strong resistance put up by the 28th Division throughout, until we finally captured the designated features.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when General Mladic arrived and General Zivanovic arrived, did you brief them with the knowledge that you had gained?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke about that when I was examined in-chief. I briefed him on the situation and all the problems with respect to the implementation of the order of the Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of any communications General Mladic had with Main Staff in Han Pijesak or the Office of the President, wherever they happened to be at the time, while he was --

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. -- while he was there at Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I was not aware of any such contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then in the evening of July 9th we have the letter authorising, under an agreement with the army, for the attack to continue, so there must have been some communication between the army and the president.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any communication with the president. Probably General Mladic did, not only when he reached the forward command post, but later on as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you provide your advice to General Zivanovic and General Mladic on the situation when they arrived on what could be done, in your opinion, based on your knowledge on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, I briefed them on the positions of the units, the problems they were having, that we had still not captured the ordered designated features, and everything else that accompanies efforts to implement the idea of the command of the Drina Corps. I cannot advise General Mladic and General Zivanovic; I simply briefed them on the situation as it was, as it stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You, as Chief of Staff of the corps, did your job and your responsibilities regarding the continuing military activities from July 9th change at all from July 9th, or did you continue to be Chief of Staff and assist in the operation as you had before?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean after General Mladic issued the order to continue the attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely, yes.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that during the examination-in-chief by the Defence regarding the role of General Mladic, the role of General Zivanovic, and myself. To provide any comments, proposals, or suggestions to General Mladic when he gave orders was quite superfluous. This was something that we were well aware of. We never even tried. Whether General Zivanovic had said anything to the Main Staff commander before that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your position as Chief of Staff would be to help facilitate and carry out the orders of your commander, General Zivanovic, and of course his commander and your commander, General Mladic. Did you continue in that role to facilitate their orders and their wishes from the time that they came to the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even General Zivanovic did not assist General Mladic, not to mention myself. We simply obeyed and did what -- listened to what General Mladic was saying to the commanders and followed what was happening, without any comments on our part. Because it was really strange -- I found it strange why he was ordering the attack to be continued and the entry into the town of Srebrenica, because it had not been indicated to anyone in any way in the order of the Corps Commander. The only task was to separate the enclaves and capture certain features, so that the units engaged in the operations should return to their original units as soon as possible and be engaged in the north-western part of the area of responsibility of the corps, towards Zivinice, Kladanj, and Olovo and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you did follow the orders of General Mladic and General Zivanovic regarding the continuing operation?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I carried out the command of the commander of Drina Corps, to carry out his decision. But as I said before, General Mladic said to both me and Zivanovic: "Look how command is done." All we could do was listen, and nothing more. On the 11th, General Mladic gave orders to General Zivanovic that he should continue the attack from Kvarc to Guber Banja, where we had problems with the Bratunac Brigade, and he ordered a unit to be brought there to continue the attack along that axis, and that was this company from the Vlasenica Brigade, consisting of 50 to 60 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, after General Mladic arrived at the forward command post, did you continue communicating to the brigades and communicating the orders of General Zivanovic in regard to the assault on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not even General Zivanovic did that, because General Mladic communicated with all the commanders and he gave them orders, and that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can see General Mladic trying to get that APC by himself off the side of the road, but did he do all the communicating with the brigade commanders by himself and continue the command and control of this operation all by himself without your assistance in any way?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After he was briefed by Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, that is, a part of his unit had entered the town, he didn't need any assistance. This was just one incident in the whole process of reaching Srebrenica. He came across this vehicle and he ordered what should be done, that another armoured vehicle should be used to pull out the UNPROFOR APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's July 11th, and I do want to get to July 11th, but we're still on July 9th. So a lot of military communication, a lot of military work had to be done to continue this attack on to Srebrenica, is that a fair statement, on July 9th?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't really a lot of work to do except to give orders to the Brigade Commanders to continue the attack and simply to monitor their progress from the forward command post, when the Brigade Commanders reported that they had accomplished the task. And from the observation post where General Mladic and General Zivanovic were, they could see those positions and monitor the progress of forces with the help of binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You had been the one that had been communicated with the Brigade Commanders and running the show prior to the arrival of General Mladic. Are you saying that you did no more of that at all after his arrival? No more communication with the Brigade Commanders on your part?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 10th, when he ordered the continuation of the assault, I did physically communicate with Brigade Commanders later on the ground where General Mladic was too, but all the actual command was taken over by General Mladic. This wasn't a broad area of attack by these units. The forces consisted of two battalions. It wasn't the whole Drina Corps that was engaged in the area for it to be necessary to communicate and monitor activities from various directions and on a broad front in the area of operations. I must repeat once again that I found it strange why such an order had been issued when the aim was, according to the Corps Commander, quite clear. I also said that General Mladic, even when down to the battalion level, even company level, wherever he went, he took over command, not only in this case, but wherever he went. There are many examples of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you do after the afternoon of July 9th when General Mladic arrived?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that I reported to him and General Zivanovic about the situation. On the 9th, we were together at the forward command post. I still had communication with all the commanders who were reporting about what they were doing, what problems they were having, how much progress they had made and so on, until the 10th, until the moment that the commanders had reported that they had accomplished the task, I monitored the course of combat operations. But the moment he arrived, he took over command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So between the 9th and the 10th, you performed your normal activities in running the operation and communicating with the Corps Commanders?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the commanders of the units that were engaged in the operation. And normally, I would send a report from the forward command post to the Drina Corps Command, regardless of the fact that General Mladic and General Zivanovic were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So with their presence, you continued your previous activities of controlling the operation under their command?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with General Mladic and General Zivanovic, and we were monitoring how his orders were being followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now I'm talking about the period between the 9th and the 10th. Who passed on General Mladic's orders?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you. I said that on the 9th, in the afternoon, and on the 10th until the moment the commanders had reported that they had accomplished the task, I communicated with them. General Mladic and General Zivanovic did not interfere in any particular way in that. They just suggested -- gave suggestions as to what should be done to speed up the dynamics of the attack and so on. But after General Mladic took over command, my role and that of General Zivanovic was a purely formal one, mere presence. We were simply present. He took over command. He called up all the commanders one by one and introduced himself. He said, "You haven't accomplished the task. I am in command now."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this occurred when? What precise date and time did General Mladic take over complete command and sideline you and General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two of them, after leaving in the evening of the 9th to spend the night somewhere, the next morning they arrived at the command post. The commanders of subordinate units reported that they had accomplished this task sometime in the morning. I don't know exactly at what time it was, but it was before noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General Krstic, just to put it in more understandable terms for us non-military people, General Mladic was commander of the whole situation. You -- General Zivanovic or you or the other commanders were supposed to implement the orders. It had to pass through you to be executed. Could I understand it this way?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. That is not so. The moment General Mladic took over command, he directly communicated with all the Brigade Commanders. He was in command of them. So what I had done before, until the moment the commanders reported that they had carried out the task of the Corps Commander, was taken over by General Mladic, and he issued commands whereas General Zivanovic and myself were just merely present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You had to be sure that the orders were executed? You had to report that mission accomplished? What was your communication? You said, "I did physically communicate with the brigade commanders." What do you mean by "physically communicate"? You were just going between the Commander-in-Chief and the lower grades?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said physically that I communicated, that was just when we entered, when we went into the town of Srebrenica and greeted one another. Until then, I couldn't be in physical contact with them. That is not what I meant before. General Mladic took over command. He gave commands to the brigade commanders. Neither myself nor General Zivanovic had any particular role in all of that from the moment he took over command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you had no role at all.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only formally. General Zivanovic was the Corps Commander. I was the Chief of Staff. But in actually in control and command of the units to continue the attack, I had no role. I have already said that I was surprised by such an order and decision to continue the attack and enter Srebrenica, because we had not planned for that. That had not been envisaged at all. There was no plan to continue the operation. So in such a situation, what kind of measures could General Zivanovic and myself undertake? It was simply the brigade commanders who went along in the direction of Srebrenica, following orders from General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just for my knowledge, according to the military rules, do officers or soldiers receive orders from the chief commander or it has to pass through the different grades?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment General Mladic appeared and took over command, even General Zivanovic, as the Corps Commander, and myself, we had no right to make any comments about it because his decision was quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: General Krstic, one question. Yesterday, you emphasised many times that the objective of Krivaja 95 was limited to reducing the size of the enclaves to the urban areas and separating them, and we should know that or we should be aware that if the objective had been any greater than that, i.e., trying to capture the town, many plans would have had to accompany it. You mentioned plans or relationships with UNPROFOR, plans for relationships with what you did with the civilians and you mentioned a whole list of those. I assume none of those were done in this case once General Mladic had said continue the attack onto the town; is that correct? None of those plans were drawn up in the usual fashion?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Not in the usual fashion, but in no fashion at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So to your knowledge, to your knowledge, there was no communication with the UN people that the objective was now to go into the town and capture it?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now going to have a break, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. McCloskey, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, now, you've testified that by -- on the 10th, when General Mladic took over what you're calling complete command, and you and General Zivanovic were completely sidelined and did not take part in the facilitation of any orders or the assisting of any orders on the continuing attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not pushed aside; we were there, where General Mladic was, and we were simply following what he was ordering to his subordinate commanders. We were not elsewhere; we were there with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you yourself do anything to implement General Mladic's orders in this time period?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nor did General Zivanovic do that, except that at one point he ordered that a company from the Vlasenica Brigade should be brought in, pursuant to the order of General Mladic that the attack from the Guber Banja axis should be stepped up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So General Zivanovic did implement General Mladic's order to bring in the Vlasenica unit?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To step up the attack in the area where the Bratunac Brigade was supposed to attack. But it didn't do that. The Bratunac Brigade wasn't acting pursuant to the order, and General Mladic said that it should be done. And then after that, General Zivanovic ordered to the Vlasenica Brigade command that a certain number of troops or units should be brought in, the units that I have already referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So how would you describe your position at this point?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I have answered your question several times already. I think I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It sounds like you were relieved of duty. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not relieved of my duty. No talk about that. But there wasn't any single order concerning the implementation of the order of the commander of the Main Staff to the brigade commanders. That was my business. This can be seen from the report which was submitted first by Vinko Pandurevic, the Zvornik commander, as he entered Srebrenica, and later on by the commanders of other brigades and units after General Mladic, together with General Zivanovic and myself, had entered the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Didn't General Mladic need your help and the help of General Zivanovic to implement the attack plan?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't request any help from us. He was in contact with all of the commanders, he monitored the activities, he issued orders, until the entry into the town. We saw on the video clip what he ordered to the commanders after they had entered the town, that is, that the attack should be continued towards Potocari and Bratunac. So he didn't issue that order to me and the Corps Commander, but directly to the brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you did absolutely nothing to implement General Mladic's orders or to assist in this continuing attack?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. McCloskey, but I do believe that I have answered your question several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you ever reactivated, where you started doing your job again and started doing your duty again?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what period you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you were, in a sense, deactivated on the 10th. So the period I'm asking about is did you remain deactivated on the 11th, on the 12th, on the 13th? When were you given responsibilities to be a general again, where you actually implemented orders from superior officers, which was your duty?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In connection with the Srebrenica operation or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Anything on those dates.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 12th or, rather, the 11th of July, when the Commander of the Main Staff ordered that an attack should be launched towards Zepa, I took over again my duty, that of the Chief of Staff of the corps, that is, the command over the units which were attacking towards Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that the evening of the 11th that you were given the job to actually do something now?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening of the 11th, at the meeting which was held at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, I received my order concerning Zepa, and my next activities were focused on the implementation of that task from then on, except for the fact that I attended the meeting at the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac, pursuant to the order of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So between the afternoon hours of July 10th, when Mladic sidelined you and Zivanovic, until the evening hours when you were assigned the Zepa operation, you did nothing?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only a report left the forward command post, and that report was forwarded to the command post of the corps and the Main Staff. So except for that order, I didn't do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to Exhibit 482A. That's a one-pager. If we could put the -- actually, if you could put the first page of the B/C/S on the ELMO very briefly, and if the General could see that B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, could you -- this is from a publication, Srpska Vojska. Could you tell us what Srpska Vojska is?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a monthly publication of the VRS, which was published by the Information Service of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In looking at the first page in the B/C/S, we see General Mladic and yourself, and I believe that's Legenda, on the podium at some sort of proceeding. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we have the same copy. I only have page 7 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I took yours and put it on the ELMO. Now, do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, perhaps we should have the English version on the ELMO. No?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, could you just tell us briefly what this -- well, we recognise General Mladic and yourself. And the man with the beret, who's that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the man with the beret?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Major Milan Jolovic, a detachment commander, the detachment in question being the Drina Wolves. They were part of the Zvornik Brigade. And as regards this stage, I believe that it took place Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. on the day when one of the professional brigades of the VRS was established, specifically this particular formation of the Drina Corps. He was appointed Commander of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And General Mladic gave a speech that day. Do you recall that speech? Do you recall hearing his speech?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I don't remember any specific details of it. But I remember that he held a speech that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, he -- according to the publication Srpska Vojska, they quote a part of the speech, and according to that, General Mladic mentions you. And I'm sorry, I can't point out to you on that exactly where that is on that first page, but if you could look for your name and I will slowly read that section in English while you have a chance to find it. And these are, according to Srpska Vojska, the words of General Mladic: "... not only in Podrinje, on Bjelasnica, Igman, Treskavica, on the Nisic plateau, but also in Krajina. You fought heroically under the leadership of your Chief of Staff or Corps Commander who, although severely wounded, made a tremendous contribution to the victory of Serbian arms and the Serbian army, not only against the Muslim gladiators in Srebrenica and Zepa, but also against those who helped them, now by land, now by air, now from behind the conference table, or through the media. They could not be saved because they did not deserve to be saved. All of those who obeyed the agreement and came to the UNPROFOR base were saved and transported." And then he goes on to talk about the buses. Now, in the beginning of this, General Mladic talks about your leading these troops first as Chief of Staff and then as Corps Commander, and he makes reference to Srebrenica and Zepa. What do you think he's talking about? First of all -- I'm sorry -- do you recall this? Do you believe this to be an accurate reflection of the speech?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When General Mladic mentions Treskavica, Bjelasnica, the Nisic plateau, he refers to the period of time of 1993 when the units of the Drina Corps took part in the Bjelasnica operation, and in late 1993 and beginning of 1994, also on the Nisic plateau, where he conducted the operations in question. At that time, I was not the commander of the Drina Corps; I was the commander of the 2nd Motorised Romanija Brigade. Earlier on in my testimony, I spoke about my activities after I had taken over as the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. That was in November and December of 1994. So at that time, General Mladic could not -- was not able to speak about that because there was no talk about that operation at that time. And in 1993 he was on Bjelasnica, and the commander of the Drina Corps at that time was General Zivanovic. So this could refer to General Zivanovic as well, who had also been severely wounded, and the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, General Skocajic. I cannot rule out the possibility that he was talking about me; however, I don't see anything in particular here, except for the mention of Treskavica, Bjelasnica, the Nisic plateau and other features that might potentially refer to me. It is true that I was in Srebrenica and in Zepa, so he -- this could actually refer to both myself and General Zivanovic or the former Chief of Staff, General Skocajic, and also perhaps to Colonel Andric, who took over as the Chief of Staff later on. So I cannot contest his words; however, he was unclear -- it was unclear who he was speaking about. General Zivanovic had been severely wounded as early as in 1992. I don't see any reason why he should be citing myself at such a ceremony, because I had only recently taken over as both the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps and the Drina Corps Commander, so it would be surprising for him to mention me and my credits without mentioning the credits of General Zivanovic and the former Chief of Staff, General Skocajic, who had been there under post since the establishment of the Drina Corps until mid-July 1995. Of course, General Skocajic had left earlier on, but he would act from time to time in the course of 1995 as Chief of Staff -- as my deputy as Chief of Staff. All Corps Commanders attended this meeting, except for General Talic, upon an invitation by General Mladic. This assembly was organised by the Main Staff and not by the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall taking the podium after General Mladic's speech?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. I spoke briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did anyone speak between you and General Mladic, or were you right after General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First the assembly was addressed by the new commander, the commander of the brigade, who had been appointed to that duty, that is, Major Jolovic; then myself as the Corps Commander; and after me, General Mladic; and then later on the others took the floor, some of those present from the army and some from the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was General Zivanovic present?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, General Zivanovic was not present at the time. He had been invited to this ceremony, but I don't know the reasons that prevented him from coming to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did General Zivanovic play any leadership role in the Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that. Before the Zepa operation started, General Zivanovic issued I don't know how many preparatory orders, what the units in Zepa should do while the operation towards Srebrenica was ongoing, and later on I would also receive from him when I reached the forward command post, I think one order from him, just for my information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So General Zivanovic didn't play much of a leadership role in Zepa; you did.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct, at the beginning of the operation and right through until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You understand it's the submission of the Prosecutor that you led the Drina Corps during the Srebrenica campaign and the events afterward, and you took over command position on the 13th, right before the Zepa operation, which is very similar to what General Mladic is saying here if you're the one he's talking about; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say whether you are right or not. Let me tell you my opinion and position and the way things were. I had no leading role in the Srebrenica operation, absolutely no leadership role whatsoever. By the Commander of the Drina Corps, I was assigned to monitor the activities of units, implementing his decision. After that -- and I also described this -- my role was sidelined after General Mladic and General Zivanovic came to the forward command post at Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, after the mentioning of the Muslim gladiators in Srebrenica and Zepa, this speech goes on to say that someone, be it you or whoever, "... also against those who helped them." Excuse me. I'll try to read that so we can make some more sense out of it. "You fought heroically under the leadership of your Chief of Staff or Corps Commander who, although severely wounded, made a tremendous contribution to the victory of Serbian arms and the Serbian army, not only against the Muslim gladiators in Srebrenica and Zepa, but also against those who helped them." Who would be those who helped the Muslims in Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence would like to object because this sentence has been taken out of the context of the whole text of this interview, and the Defence would request that when asking questions, the Prosecutor be more specific regarding time and persons he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm trying to be as specific as I can relating to the wording of the document, and if the General needs to take more time to review the whole article, I have no objection to that. The General has taken some time, I believe, and put us in the context that the Nisic plateau and the Krajina had nothing to do with him. Therefore, it's this next few sentences, starting with "You fought heroically ..." that I wish to direct his attention at. I think he has helped us, through his testimony, pinpoint the area that he may or may not be involved in, but I would like to ask his viewpoint on these particular words to see if he can help us understand them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we will wait for the answer of General Krstic. It is all part of the general context of the question, the dates and persons that are referred to. So let us wait for the answer of the General regarding persons and dates. They will be part of the answer. If not, we'll see. If not, Mr. McCloskey can be more specific in his questions. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, do you need to read the whole article to get a feeling for the context of these sentences, or do you want to take a little time to do that, or do you feel you understand the speech and can answer my questions?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your part of the question, but would you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And again because it's a long sentence, I better start from the beginning.
